I'm known for it. But lately, oh my goodness, I’m getting all the appointment times wrong. I’ll call poor Betty twice in one morning, and she’ll tell me we just spoke ten minutes ago, and I just... I feel so foolish because my thoughts are just so muddled and thick. Well, yes, actually. Now that you mention it, my mood has been... well, it’s just been terribly flat. Down, I suppose you could say. It’s funny you ask about losing interest, because that’s exactly what my daughter said to me just the other day when she came over to bring me some groceries. I have this lovely set of Windsor and Newton paints my late husband bought me for our fortieth anniversary, and I usually just love blending the colors, especially for the spring flowers. But lately, the box just sits there on the side table, gathering dust, and I look at it and I just... I can't make myself care. 

And it's not just the painting, either. It's everything. My tomato plants out on the patio, the little cherry ones that usually do so well this time of year—I haven't even been out to water them. They're probably all shriveled up by now, which is a shame because I usually make a wonderful fresh salsa for the heritage center potlucks. I haven't been to my line dancing class at the senior center, either. I've gone every Wednesday morning for five years, rain or shine, but the thought of putting on my shoes and trying to follow the steps... it just feels like climbing a mountain. Even the little things, like watching the cardinals out back. I have two feeders, you know, one for suet and one for sunflower seeds, and I usually sit with my morning tea and just watch them bicker over the best spots. They’re such beautiful, bright red birds, usually they bring me so much joy. But now, I just sit in my chair, staring out the glass, and I see them fluttering around, but I don't feel anything at all. It's just so strange, Doctor, to look at all these things that used to fill up my days and make me so happy, and just feel absolutely nothing towards them. It’s like someone just turned the color down on my whole life, if that makes any sense.

Oh, making decisions... and planning... yes, it's just been a complete disaster, to be perfectly honest with you. It really has. I mean, I’ve actually been missing my own appointments, which is so terribly unlike me. Just last month, I was supposed to see Dr. Miller—he's my podiatrist, you know, I've been seeing him for my arches for years and years. I had the little reminder card they give you, the one with the date and time written on the back, and I pinned it right to the corkboard by the telephone where I put everything important. But when the day came, I just couldn't seem to organize my morning, didn't even look at the calendar, and I missed the visit entirely. They had to call and ask where I was, and I was just sitting in my armchair in my robe. 

And the organizing at the center... well, I mentioned the schedule earlier, but it's worse than just calling the wrong person. I’ve tangled up the senior center schedule so badly that it's practically unusable. I had three people scheduled to work the front desk on Tuesday morning, and absolutely nobody on Thursday, which is our busiest day because of the weekly bingo. I used to be able to look at a grid and just know exactly who goes where, but now, looking at all those names and times, my brain just freezes. I can't decide who to put in which slot, and I just get so overwhelmed. 

It’s gotten so bad that my husband has had to step in and take over for me. Bless him, he’s not usually one for paperwork—he's always left the administrative things to me—but he’s been having to help with all the phone calls and keeping the calendars straight just so we know what day it is and who needs to be where. And it's not even just the schedules, it's things around the house, too. The washing machine started making this dreadful clanking noise last week, right in the middle of the spin cycle. Usually, I'd just look up the repair service, compare a few places, and make a decision on who to call. I've always handled that sort of thing. But I just stood there in the laundry room listening to it clank, and I couldn't figure out what step to take first. I couldn't make a single decision about it. My husband finally had to just take the phone and handle the repair decisions himself. It just makes me feel so entirely useless, Doctor, to have him doing all these things I used to handle myself without batting an eye... it's just not me.

Oh, heavens, no. No, nothing like that, thank goodness. I mean, I might forget why I walked into the kitchen, like I told you with the tissues and the flour, but I certainly know it’s *my* kitchen. We’ve lived in this house on Maple Drive since... oh, it must be 1978, right after my daughter started kindergarten. It has that lovely bay window in the front that looks out at the oak tree. So I always know exactly where I am, I've never gotten lost or wandered off or anything frightening like that. 

And as for what day it is... well, even when I missed my podiatrist appointment with Dr. Miller, it wasn't because I thought it was Wednesday instead of Thursday. I knew perfectly well it was Thursday, I just... I just couldn't get myself out of my chair and organized enough to go. But I always know the days. You sort of have to keep track of the rhythm of the week, don't you? The trash and recycling get picked up on Wednesday mornings, so my husband always rolls the big green bins down the driveway on Tuesday nights right after Jeopardy, just like clockwork. 

And people... oh, I would be absolutely terrified if I didn't know who I was speaking to. I know my husband, I know my daughter, I know Gary the postman. I know it's you I'm talking to right now. I had an aunt, my mother's older sister, Aunt Mildred, and she got like that toward the end of her life, bless her heart. She used to look right at me and call me Eleanor, which was my mother's name. She would hold my hand and ask me when the war was going to be over. It was just heartbreaking to see her sitting in her favorite floral armchair, completely lost in her own living room, not knowing her own family or what decade it was. So, no, I watch out for that sort of thing, and I can tell you for a fact I haven't had any trouble knowing who people are or where I am. It's just the short-term things, the mail and the pantry and the schedules, that slip right through the cracks. But the big things, the who and the where and the when, those are all still right where they belong.

It just makes me feel so entirely useless, Doctor, to have him doing all these things I used to handle myself without batting an eye... it's just not me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself confused about where you are, what day it is, or who you're speaking to?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, no. So I always know exactly where I am, I've never gotten lost or wandered off or anything frightening like that. \n\nAnd as for what day it is... well, even when I missed my podiatrist appointment with Dr. Miller, it wasn't because I thought it was Wednesday instead of Thursday. I knew perfectly well it was Thursday, I just... I just couldn't get myself out of my chair and organized enough to go. But I always know the days. You sort of have to keep track of the rhythm of the week, don't you? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, it was definitely me who noticed it first. I mean... I'm the one living in this brain, aren't I? It's just so terribly frustrating because I've always prided myself on being sharp as a tack. I remember back when I was organizing the school bake sales—this was when my daughter was in middle school, so ages and ages ago—and I could keep dozens of pastry orders straight in my head without writing a single one down. I just knew exactly who wanted the cherry pie and who needed the gluten-free brownies. 

So when I started standing in the kitchen staring at the flour, or holding the mail out by the empty box like a complete fool, well, I knew right away something wasn't right. I felt it immediately. It's like a heavy fog just rolls in out of nowhere. Now, my husband, he did start noticing it too, of course. How could he not? Especially with the washing machine incident and the senior center schedules I told you about. He actually said to me the other evening—we were sitting in the living room, he was reading the evening paper and I was trying to knit a scarf for my granddaughter, just a simple garter stitch but I kept losing my place and having to count my rows over and over—and he put his paper down, took his reading glasses off, and said I seemed a bit scattered lately. 

But I already knew! I told him, I said, "I feel like my brain is just full of cotton wool!" So it certainly wasn't a surprise to me when he brought it up. I haven't been oblivious to it, if that's what you're asking. Some people, like my Aunt Mildred I mentioned earlier, they don't even know they're forgetting things. They just live in their own little world and the rest of us just have to adapt to it. But me? Oh, I feel every single little slip. It's just a dreadful feeling, knowing you're messing things up and not being able to stop it, just watching yourself forget what you were doing right in the middle of doing it. I'm very aware of it, Doctor, painfully aware, to be completely honest with you. It's just me who feels it the most.

I've gone every Wednesday morning for five years, rain or shine, but the thought of putting on my shoes and trying to follow the steps... it just feels like climbing a mountain. Even the little things, like watching the cardinals out back. I have two feeders, you know, one for suet and one for sunflower seeds, and I usually sit with my morning tea and just watch them bicker over the best spots. They’re such beautiful, bright red birds, usually they bring me so much joy. But now, I just sit in my chair, staring out the glass, and I see them fluttering around, but I don't feel anything at all. It's just so strange, Doctor, to look at all these things that used to fill up my days and make me so happy, and just feel absolutely nothing towards them. It’s like someone just turned the color down on my whole life, if that makes any sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any trouble remembering things, like recent events, names of people you know well, or how to do everyday tasks?\n\nPatient: Well, remembering things... I suppose that goes right back to what I was saying earlier about the heritage center, doesn't it? It's just... it's all so mixed up. But as for names of people I know well, or everyday tasks... no, I wouldn't say I've forgotten my own daughter's name, or how to make a cup of tea, thank goodness. \n\nBut it's the little things that just slip away. Like the other morning, I went into the kitchen to get a fresh box of tissues—I always keep the extras in the pantry, right next to the baking supplies, top shelf, because you never know when you'll need one, especially with the dust we've been having lately. So I walked in there, opened the pantry door, and I just stood there. Stood there staring at the flour and the sugar, and I had absolutely no earthly idea what I had gone in there for. I must have stood there for five whole minutes, just looking at the shelves. I even picked up a can of crushed tomatoes, thinking maybe I was going to make sauce, but it was 8:00 in the morning! Who makes sauce at 8:00 in the morning? \n\nAnd then there was the business with the mail. I always get the mail right after lunch, around 1:30. The postman, Gary, he's such a nice young man, always waves when he drives by. Well, I walked out to the box, brought the mail in, set it on the kitchen counter right next to the fruit bowl—I have this beautiful ceramic bowl my sister got me in New Mexico, painted with little blue quail—anyway, I set it down. Not two hours later, I was putting my shoes on to go out and get the mail. I walked all the way down the driveway, opened the empty box, and felt so confused. I came back inside and there it all was, sitting right next to the quail bowl. It’s just so unsettling, Doctor. It’s not that I don't know who people are, it's just that my brain feels like a sieve, and all the recent things just fall right through before I can catch them.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulties with planning, organizing, or making decisions lately?\n\nPatient: Oh, making decisions... and planning... yes, it's just been a complete disaster, to be perfectly honest with you. Just last month, I was supposed to see Dr. Miller—he's my podiatrist, you know, I've been seeing him for my arches for years and years. They had to call and ask where I was, and I was just sitting in my armchair in my robe. \n\nAnd the organizing at the center... well, I mentioned the schedule earlier, but it's worse than just calling the wrong person. My husband finally had to just take the phone and handle the repair decisions himself. It just makes me feel so entirely useless, Doctor, to have him doing all these things I used to handle myself without batting an eye... it's just not me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself confused about where you are, what day it is, or who you're speaking to?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, no. I knew perfectly well it was Thursday, I just... I just couldn't get myself out of my chair and organized enough to go. But I always know the days. I know my husband, I know my daughter, I know Gary the postman. I know it's you I'm talking to right now. I had an aunt, my mother's older sister, Aunt Mildred, and she got like that toward the end of her life, bless her heart. She used to look right at me and call me Eleanor, which was my mother's name. She would hold my hand and ask me when the war was going to be over. It was just heartbreaking to see her sitting in her favorite floral armchair, completely lost in her own living room, not knowing her own family or what decade it was. It's just the short-term things, the mail and the pantry and the schedules, that slip right through the cracks. But the big things, the who and the where and the when, those are all still right where they belong.\n\nDoctor: Doctor: Have you ever felt like something was wrong with your memory or thinking, or did you feel like other people were noticing it more than you did yourself?\n\nPatient: Oh, it was definitely me who noticed it first. Oh, seeing or hearing things? Like hallucinations? No, no, I haven't had anything like that at all. Goodness, that sounds frightening. Well, let me think about that... suddenly or slowly. I'd have to say it was more of a... a slow slide downhill, if that makes sense. It certainly didn't just happen overnight, like flipping a light switch. The whole thing, the really difficult part with my thinking and feeling so overwhelmed, has been going on for about four months now.

Oh, my, yes. Much, much longer than two weeks, unfortunately. Like I was just saying about that dreadful water damage and the remodel—that all started four months ago, and at first it was just the stress of it all, you know, my thoughts getting all jumbled up with the noise and the workmen coming and going and the dust everywhere. Some people, like my Aunt Mildred I mentioned earlier, they don't even know they're forgetting things. They just live in their own little world and the rest of us just have to adapt to it. But me? Oh, I feel every single little slip. It's just a dreadful feeling, knowing you're messing things up and not being able to stop it, just watching yourself forget what you were doing right in the middle of doing it. I'm very aware of it, Doctor, painfully aware, to be completely honest with you. It's just me who feels it the most.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any weakness, numbness, or difficulty with coordination, balance, or vision that comes and goes or has been getting worse?\n\nPatient: Oh, weakness or numbness? No, no, nothing like that at all, thank goodness. My balance is actually quite good for a woman my age. I mean, I still walk down the long part of the driveway to get the morning paper every single day, rain or shine. Well, maybe not when it's icy out, my husband absolutely refuses to let me out the front door when it's freezing rain because he worries I'll slip and break a hip—you hear such terrible stories about women my age taking a tumble and never quite recovering—but my coordination itself is perfectly fine. I don't feel unsteady on my feet or clumsy at all. Just the usual drugstore readers. I buy them by the handful at the pharmacy on the corner and leave a pair in the kitchen, a pair by my floral armchair, a pair on the nightstand... but my actual eyesight hasn't suddenly changed or gotten blurry or anything frightening like that. \n\nI certainly don't have any tingling or numbness in my fingers or my toes, either. Physically, my body feels quite strong, really. I still do the light dusting and water all my African violets without any trouble holding the watering can. It's just so terribly frustrating because my arms and legs work perfectly well and will do exactly what I tell them to do, it's just that my brain has stopped knowing what to tell them! So, no, no physical weakness or balance issues or anything like that. Just that awful cotton wool feeling in my head.\n\nDoctor: Have you had days where you felt down or hopeless nearly every day, and if so, how often and for how long have you felt that way?\n\nPatient: Down or hopeless... oh, heavens, yes. I wake up in the morning, and the sun might be shining, and I can hear the birds out by the feeder, but I just think, 'Oh, dear, another whole day to have to get through.' \n\nMy husband, bless his heart, he tries so hard to cheer me up. He’ll say, 'Let’s go for a little drive,' or he'll offer to make me a nice cup of chamomile tea, but I just don’t have the heart for any of it. I really don't. It's like all the color has just washed right out of the world, and everything takes so much effort. Just standing up to go to the kitchen feels like a monumental task. \n\nAnd as for how long it's been going on... well, I’ve been thinking about this, trying to pin it down for you. Oh, heavens, four days... you know, I really couldn't give you a precise number like that.
